# Building Ring Out on the Steam Deck, start to finish

Everything happens on the Deck. No second machine.

**Tested on**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Hardware | Steam Deck LCD (`Jupiter`) |
| SteamOS | **3.8.25**, build `20260807.2` |
| Kernel | 6.18.42-valve2-1-neptune-618 |
| Toolchain | gcc 15.1.1, cmake 4.0.3, ninja 1.12.1, python3 3.13.5 |
| Package | RingOut 1.4 |

SteamOS moves, and it moves the things this depends on: a system update wipes
anything installed into `/usr`, and a newer Arch snapshot can change compiler
versions under you. If your SteamOS is much newer than the above and something
here does not match, that is the first thing to suspect — particularly section
6, which is entirely about SteamOS's packaging behaviour.

Two packages are involved and they do different jobs:

* **`RingOut-1.4-linux`** — the desktop package. You do not *play* with this on
  the Deck (it bundles 66 libraries that fight the Deck's own Mesa driver), but
  it is the only one that can BUILD, because it carries `module-src/`.
* **`RingOut-1.4-deck`** — the Deck package. This is what you play with. It
  ships no game data, so you copy the two things you built into it.

You also need **your own disc image**. `.iso`, `.gcm`, `.wbfs`, `.rvz`, `.gcz`
and NKit variants all work.

---

## 0. Check the Deck can build (once, and after every SteamOS update)

```sh
for t in clang gcc cmake ninja python3; do printf '%-8s ' "$t"; command -v $t || echo MISSING; done
printf '#include <stdatomic.h>\n#include <math.h>\nint main(void){return 0;}\n' > /tmp/probe.c
cc /tmp/probe.c -o /tmp/probe && echo "compiler+headers OK"
```

The second command is the real test. Checking for `/usr/include/stdio.h` is not
enough and checking `/usr/include/stdatomic.h` is actively misleading — that one
ships with the COMPILER (`/usr/lib/clang/20/include/`), not with glibc, so it is
absent whenever no compiler is installed and present the moment one is.
Compiling something is the only check that covers both halves.

If any is MISSING, or `stdio.h` is not there, do section 6 first.

**The shipped profiles need clang 22 or newer.** They are generated by LLVM 22,
and an indexed profile can only be read by an LLVM at least as new as the one
that wrote it. SteamOS 3.8 ships clang 20, so on a stock Deck the build reports

```
module: this clang cannot read the shipped PGO profile
```

and continues without it — correct module, about 13% slower. That is a real
limitation of this release, not something you have done wrong. **Confirmed on
this Deck**: the PAL build offered `module-src/profiles/GRSPAF.profdata`, clang
20 refused it, and the module came out 23 MB instead of the 39 MB a profiled
build produces.

**You can get the 13% back on the Deck itself** — see section 2b. There is no
single profile file that would work here: even a readable one matches functions
by a hash the *instrumenting* compiler computed, so a profile made by a
different clang has its counts thrown away. The profile has to be made by the
clang doing the build, which means making it on the Deck.

**clang is still worth having, not optional-in-practice.** The build works with gcc,
but the profile-guided step is clang-only — both `setup.sh` and the module's
CMakeLists check for it — so a gcc build silently forfeits about 13% of CPU
time. It will say `no profile ships for <ID>` even when one did ship. A SteamOS
update wipes all of it, so expect to repeat that section occasionally.

## 1. Unpack

```sh
cd ~
unzip RingOut-1.4-linux-x86_64.zip
unzip RingOut-1.4-steamdeck-x86_64.zip
```

## 2. Build your module

```sh
cd ~/RingOut-1.4-linux
./setup.sh --deck /path/to/your/disc.rvz
```

**`--deck` is not optional here.** Without it the module is compiled for the
machine that built it; with it, `-march=x86-64-v3`, which is what a Deck's Zen 2
can execute. It also checks the result and tells you if something is wrong.

This takes roughly 15 minutes: it extracts the disc, recompiles the game's
executable into C, and compiles that into a module. It ends with

```
Deck-compatible: -march=x86-64-v3, glibc floor 2.4.
Copy game/ and bin/gGRSxAF_recomp.so into the Deck package.
Setup complete.
```

If the extract step says `unsupported format`, your image is `.rvz`/`.gcz`/`.wia`.
Use the runtime's extractor instead and re-run:

```sh
./bin/moderngekko-run --extract /path/to/your/disc.rvz ./game
./setup.sh --deck /path/to/your/disc.rvz
```

## 2b. (Optional) Get the 13% back

The build above is correct but unprofiled. To train a profile with the clang you
actually have:

```sh
sudo pacman -S llvm                   # for llvm-profdata -- NOT --needed, see section 6
cd ~/RingOut-1.4-linux
./setup.sh --deck --pgo /path/to/your/disc.rvz
```

It builds a second, instrumented module, plays 6000 frames of an arcade match
headless to collect counts, merges them, and rebuilds. You will see

```
==> 4/4  Training a profile with YOUR clang (one time only)
    Measured: ~11 minutes on a desktop, on top of a normal build.
    A Steam Deck is a good deal slower -- leave it running.
    playing 6000 frames to collect counts ...
    rebuilding with your own profile ...
    done -- built with a profile trained on your own machine.
```

**How long on a Deck?** Measured, on this Deck, PAL, start to finish:

| phase | time |
|---|---|
| extract + recompile + plain module | 7m 24s |
| instrumented build | 8m 27s |
| training run, 6000 frames | 1m 25s |
| profiled rebuild | ~16m |
| **total** | **33m 53s** |

So about 26 minutes on top of a normal build. Start it and go and do something
else; there is nothing to press.

## Is it worth doing?

**For**

* 14% less CPU time, measured on THIS Deck with the profile it trained
  itself: 233.99 → 201.07 Gcyc over 6000 fixed frames, 8 runs an arm, the two
  ranges not overlapping at all, every run hashing identically. Wall clock
  75.5s → 68.3s for the same work, and IPC 2.005 → 2.136. That is the margin
  that decides whether the heavier stages hold 60.
* A profile you train here beats the one that ships — 1.2% ahead on a desktop
  A/B, ranges not overlapping over six runs each, because it matches your
  compiler exactly instead of being written by a newer one.
* Speed only. Guest state is untouched: 18 benchmark runs, profiled and not,
  produced one identical hash. Saves, netplay and replays are unaffected.

**Against**

* ~26 minutes, once.
* Needs `clang` and `llvm-profdata` (the `llvm` package). gcc cannot do it.
* Needs save data to train against — see below.
* The module roughly doubles on disk, 23 MB → 39 MB.
* The profile belongs to ONE disc. A different region means training again.

You never have to do this. The unprofiled module is correct and plays fine.

The finished module is noticeably bigger (about 39 MB rather than 23 MB); that
is the profiled codegen, and it is how you can tell at a glance which one you
have.

**Play the game once before you run this.** The training route needs your save
data to get past the memory-card screen. Measured on this exact route and
module, the only difference being the save file:

| | prims/frame | draws/frame | what it was doing |
|---|---|---|---|
| no save | 397 | 2.4 | sat on the memory-card screen |
| with save | 21547 | 84.1 | playing the match |

A fresh package ships no save — deliberately, it is your data, not something
that can come from someone else's card. One session that writes one is enough;
it lands in `userdata/GC/` and `--pgo` picks it up on its own.

If it says `the training run never reached a match`, that is what happened, and
it keeps your existing module on purpose: a profile trained on a menu builds
something *slower* than no profile at all.

Everything here is optional. A module built without it plays fine.

## Messages during the build that are NOT problems

**`Performing Test MODULE_LLD_USABLE - Failed`** — expected on a stock Deck.
`lld` is a separate package from clang on Arch, so it is simply not there, and
the build probes for it rather than assuming. Without it the module links with
the ordinary linker, which was measured at 144.3s against lld's 144.5s — a 0.1%
gap inside a 1% spread, i.e. nothing. lld is only wanted for the ThinLTO cache,
and `setup.sh` wipes `work/` on every run so that cache never applies. Installing
lld is not worth doing.

**`module: this clang cannot read the shipped PGO profile`** — expected too, and
the one that actually costs you something. See section 2b.

## 3. Move it into the Deck package

`setup.sh --deck` does this for you when it can see exactly one Deck package
beside the one you built in, and says so:

```
Installing into RingOut-1.4-deck ...
done: game/ and gGRSPAF_recomp.so are in RingOut-1.4-deck.
```

If it printed the two `cp` commands instead, it found no Deck package or more
than one. Run them yourself:

```sh
cd ~/ringout-build
cp -r RingOut-1.4-linux/game             RingOut-1.4-deck/
cp    RingOut-1.4-linux/bin/g*_recomp.so RingOut-1.4-deck/bin/
```

## 4. Play

```sh
cd ~/RingOut-1.4-deck
./RingOut
```

For Game Mode: Desktop Mode → Steam → Games → Add a Non-Steam Game → browse to
`~/RingOut-1.4-deck/RingOut`. Then launch it from Game Mode like any other game.

## 5. Check it worked

```sh
cd ~/RingOut-1.4-deck
RINGOUT_DETERMINISM_LOG=/tmp/h.log RINGOUT_DETERMINISM_FRAMES=1500 \
  ./bin/moderngekko-run --headless --user-dir ./userdata \
    --game ./game --module ./bin/g*_recomp.so
wc -l /tmp/h.log
```

`[staticrecomp] module loaded:` and 1500 lines means the module is good. This
does not need a display, so it works over ssh.

---

## 6. If the toolchain is missing

SteamOS ships no compiler and mounts `/usr` read-only.

```sh
sudo steamos-readonly disable
sudo pacman-key --init
sudo pacman-key --populate archlinux
sudo pacman -S base-devel clang glibc linux-api-headers cmake ninja
```

Add `llvm` to that list if you want section 2b. Installing `clang` does **not**
give you `llvm-profdata` — checked on this Deck, `clang` 20.1.8 was installed and
`llvm-profdata` was still missing, because it lives in the separate `llvm`
package. Nothing else needs it, so leave it out if you are skipping 2b.

**Do not add `--needed`.** SteamOS ships `/usr/include` stripped while leaving
the packages registered as installed — pacman's database claims glibc owns 504
headers when 14 are on disk. With `--needed` it decides everything is present,
installs nothing, and you get compilers with no headers. That failure appears
much later, during the build, and looks like something else entirely.

**Never `-Sy` or `-Syu`.** SteamOS pins snapshot repos; without `-Sy` you are
restoring files at the version you already have, which is safe. With it you can
pull a newer snapshot, and that is what actually breaks Decks.

Re-enable read-only afterwards if you like: `sudo steamos-readonly enable`.
A SteamOS update wipes everything installed this way. The module you built
survives — it is just a file.

---

## What each command is for

| Command | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `./setup.sh --deck <disc>` | extract + recompile + build the module, targeted at Zen 2 |
| `./bin/moderngekko-run --extract <disc> ./game` | extract formats the recompiler cannot read (`.rvz`, `.gcz`, `.wia`) |
| `./RingOut` | launch the game |
| `./bin/moderngekko-run --headless ...` | verify without a display |
| `./tools/dolrecomp --gamecube <dol> --idle-pc auto -jN <out>` | the recompile step alone, if you want to run it by hand |

## Notes

* Building a second region is safe: the launcher picks the module matching the
  disc in `game/`, so a US and a PAL module can sit in `bin/` together.
* The cheat lists install themselves into `userdata/GameSettings/` on first run —
  23 codes for the US disc, 35 for the Japanese, 177 for the European. All
  listed, none enabled; turn on what you want from the CHEATS tab (Escape).
* The build picks a profile matching your disc automatically, worth about 13%
  (measured on this Deck: 493.52 Gcyc without, 429.30 Gcyc with). **This needs
  clang** — with gcc you get a correct but slower module, and the only sign is
  the line `no profile ships for <ID>` during setup. A disc with genuinely no
  profile builds without one, which is correct: another region's profile
  measured *worse* than none.
